cim: Anthropic: The ever more dizzying gamble of AI
cim_eredeti: Anthropic: The ever more dizzying gamble of AI
szoveg_eredeti:
Artificial intelligence (AI) has less and less room for disappointment. While investors have been questioning the profitability promises of this technology, Anthropic pulled off, on Thursday, November 19, the largest initial public offering in history, raising $81 billion. The stock rose by 17% on its first day of trading, only to drop by 8.5% the next day in a market rout that saw the Nasdaq lose 5.3%, erasing its gains since January 1. Five months after SpaceX arrived on Wall Street and with anticipation building for OpenAI's debut, the event adds a new dimension to American capitalism's bet on AI. But behind this display of power, new vulnerabilities are emerging.

The sums raised by Anthropic may seem extravagant, but so are its financial needs. Now holding $230 billion (€210 billion) in cash, the company plans to allocate $900 billion to its computing infrastructure by 2045. As spectacular as it is, its revenue growth will need to remain robust for years to make such investments profitable. This is a tall order.

The development of AI is also characterized by the growing interdependence of its players. Nvidia, Microsoft and Google, some of Anthropic's main suppliers, are also among its backers. From semiconductor manufacturers to electricity providers, banks and investment funds, entire sectors of the economy are pinning their growth hopes on the same assumptions. If these are called into question, it could trigger a domino effect, impacting both industrial investment and the value of global savings.

The strength of the US economy already owes much to AI-related investments and the wealth effects driven by the surge in tech stocks. But this momentum has brought rising tensions over energy prices and certain types of equipment, while the cost of funding is undermining projects with uncertain profitability. Friday's market correction offered a glimpse of these risks. Investors have anticipated AI profits to such an extent that even a slight mismatch between expectations and actual revenues can be enough to cause a reversal.

Investors must also contend with growing opposition to the construction of data centers, as illustrated by the midterm election campaign. Whether this infrastructure can be deployed at the planned pace will depend on what the public is willing to accept.

Some industry players themselves recognize the need to set limits on this expansion. Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei pledged not to give in to commercial or political pressures, even if that means slowing down the development of the company's models for safety reasons. Publicly listed companies' transparency obligations may encourage better oversight of this sector. But how much leeway will executives have to put the brakes on the race for ever more powerful models if economic prosperity and the value of savings increasingly depend on it?

The danger would be that AI could become so indispensable to economic prosperity that public authorities lose their ability to regulate it from both technological and environmental perspectives.
